prompt: Ana's code works against labembed. What does she change to run it against OpenAI's real service?
hint: The lesson lists what changes and says nothing else does.

choices.text: Rewrite the calls with `requests`, since the SDK only talks to the lab
choices.why: The SDK is OpenAI's own library; the lab was built so that it needs no changes. Its default address is OpenAI's.

choices.text: Drop OPENAI_BASE_URL, use her own key, and name text-embedding-3-small
choices.why: Right. The base URL, the key and the model name are the only differences; the calls stay the same.

choices.text: Install a different version of the openai package
choices.why: The same version talks to both. Nothing in the package is specific to the lab.

choices.text: Add `encoding_format="base64"` to every call
choices.why: The SDK already adds it on its own, against the lab and against OpenAI alike.

prompt: Which description of labembed matches the lesson?
hint: Separate what is real from what is imitated.

choices.text: A recording of real OpenAI responses, replayed for each request
choices.why: Nothing was recorded from OpenAI; no provider could be reached. Every vector is computed when the request arrives.

choices.text: OpenAI's own open-source server, run locally
choices.why: OpenAI publishes no such server. labembed was written for the course.

choices.text: A course-written server in OpenAI's format, serving real vectors from two local models
choices.why: Right. The wire format is imitated; the vectors come from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and WordLlama, under the lab's own names.

choices.text: A proxy that forwards requests to OpenAI and caches the vectors
choices.why: It forwards nothing anywhere. The machine could not reach OpenAI at all.

prompt: In the lab, asking for `text-embedding-3-small` raised `NotFoundError` with status 404. Why?
hint: Read the message labembed sent back.

choices.text: The model was retired by OpenAI
choices.why: text-embedding-3-small is on the price sheet and is the name to use against OpenAI. The refusal is the lab's.

choices.text: The key in the environment has no access to that model
choices.why: A key problem is a 401, as the first refusal showed. This was a 404 about the model name.

choices.text: labembed refuses real model names so that no lab vector passes as OpenAI's
choices.why: Right. It serves lab-minilm and lab-wordllama and nothing else, on purpose.

choices.text: The SDK spells the name differently and the server cannot find it
choices.why: The SDK sends the name exactly as written, as the raw request body showed in the next section.

prompt: With curl, the key travels in the header `Authorization: ___ $OPENAI_API_KEY`.
hint: The same word appears before every OpenAI key in that header.

prompt: Where in an embeddings response is the vector for the second text of the input list?
hint: Look at what response.py printed for each object.

choices.text: In the `data` object whose `index` is 1
choices.why: Right. Each object carries the position of its text, counting from 0, and its `embedding`.

choices.text: In `usage`, next to the token count
choices.why: `usage` holds only counts of tokens. The vectors are in `data`.

choices.text: In a second response, since the API returns one response per text
choices.why: One request with three texts returned one response with three objects in `data`.

choices.text: In `model`, which lists the vectors the model produced
choices.why: `model` is just the model's name, lab-minilm here.

prompt: The objects in `data` came back in the order of the inputs. Why does the lesson still sort by `index`?
hint: What would a mistake look like if the order ever differed?

choices.text: Sorting makes the vectors normalised
choices.why: Sorting changes their order, not their values. They arrive at length 1 already.

choices.text: The index is the field that names the text; position is an arrangement nobody checks
choices.why: Right. Filed by position, a vector out of place would sit under the wrong article and raise no error.

choices.text: The SDK returns them in reverse order unless they are sorted
choices.why: response.py printed them in order 0, 1, 2 without sorting.

choices.text: Sorting is required before the vectors can be stored
choices.why: Nothing requires it. It is how you make sure each vector is stored against the right text.

prompt: The raw request body showed `"encoding_format": "base64"`, which Ana's code never wrote. What happened?
hint: Compare what crossed the wire with what the SDK handed over.

choices.text: The lab rewrote the request because it cannot send floats
choices.why: labembed sends floats when asked: the first curl call, with no encoding_format, got a list of numbers.

choices.text: The SDK asked for base64 to shrink the response, then decoded it into floats
choices.why: Right. The decoded bytes matched the SDK's list exactly, and the base64 answer was much smaller.

choices.text: Base64 is required by OpenAI's API, so every client must send it
choices.why: The default is float; curl got numbers without asking. Base64 is an option the SDK chooses.

choices.text: The SDK compresses the input text before sending it
choices.why: The input went as plain text in the JSON body. Base64 applies to the vectors coming back.

prompt: text-embedding-3-small returns 1,536 numbers. Sent as little-endian float32 and encoded in base64 (4 characters for every 3 bytes), how many characters is one vector?
hint: First the bytes: 4 per float32.

prompt: Put in order what happens to one vector between the server and Ana's list of floats, when she calls the SDK.
hint: The request leaves before the vector exists.
items: The SDK sends the request with encoding_format set to base64
The server writes its float32 bytes as base64 text in the JSON
The SDK decodes the base64 back into bytes
The SDK reads the bytes as little-endian float32 and returns a list
trap: The base64 text is written by the server and decoded by the SDK: decoding comes after the JSON arrives, not before the request leaves.

prompt: A batch of 500 texts includes one empty string. What happens to the request?
hint: Look at limits.py's first line.

choices.text: The empty string gets a zero vector and the rest are embedded
choices.why: There is no zero vector: the server refused the request with a 400.

choices.text: The empty string is skipped and 499 vectors come back
choices.why: Nothing is skipped. The index of every other vector would then be ambiguous, and the server refuses instead.

choices.text: The whole request is refused with 400
choices.why: Right. One blank text loses the other 499, so filter empty texts out before sending.

choices.text: The SDK retries until the server accepts it
choices.why: A 400 is not retried: sending the same request again gets the same answer.

prompt: tiktoken counted 2,205 tokens in the help centre, but labembed's log added up to a different number. Why?
hint: Who counted each number, and with what?

choices.text: labembed counts characters, not tokens
choices.why: It counts tokens, but with a different tokeniser. Characters would give a far larger number.

choices.text: tiktoken skips the titles of the articles
choices.why: batch.py counted title and body together, the same text that was sent.

choices.text: Each count uses a different model's tokeniser
choices.why: Right. A bill is counted with the provider's tokeniser, so estimate with the provider's counter and check against usage.

choices.text: Some requests were sent twice and counted twice
choices.why: The log shows exactly three requests, 16, 16 and 8 texts. Nothing was repeated.

prompt: OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models count tokens with tiktoken's ___ encoding.
hint: Its name starts with cl and ends with base.

prompt: What does `dimensions=128` ask a text-embedding-3 model for?
hint: Compare with what dims.py measured.

choices.text: A vector of 128 numbers, renormalised to length 1
choices.why: Right. The server keeps the first 128 coordinates and divides by their length, which is why the API's vectors and the hand-renormalised ones matched.

choices.text: The 128 texts most similar to the input
choices.why: That is a search, which the embeddings endpoint does not do. It returns vectors, not neighbours.

choices.text: A vector computed by a smaller, cheaper model
choices.why: Same model, same price per token; the request names the model, and the parameter only shortens its output.

choices.text: A vector with 128 bits per number instead of 32
choices.why: The numbers stay float32. The parameter changes how many there are.

prompt: Ana keeps the first 64 of WordLlama's 256 numbers herself and ranks by dot product without renormalising. What goes wrong?
hint: What did dims.py print about the lengths?

choices.text: Nothing: a dot product ignores length
choices.why: A dot product grows with length, as lesson 2 showed. That is why the lengths matter here.

choices.text: The vectors become 64 bytes each, too small to compare
choices.why: 64 float32 numbers are 256 bytes, and the API's 64-number vectors compared fine.

choices.text: The search crashes because the lengths differ
choices.why: Nothing crashes. The ranking quietly gets worse, which is harder to notice.

choices.text: The cut vectors have different lengths, so long ones win for being long
choices.why: Right. Renormalised, the same cut vectors match the API's, question for question.

prompt: A team stores 768-number vectors from an open model and plans to cut them to 256 to save space, the way `dimensions` does. What should they check first?
hint: Why could lab-wordllama be cut and lab-minilm not?

choices.text: That the vectors are float32 and not float16
choices.why: The number type does not decide whether a prefix is useful. How the model was trained does.

choices.text: Whether the model was trained so that its first coordinates work alone
choices.why: Right. Without that training a prefix keeps an arbitrary part of what the model learned. Measure recall at 256 on their own questions too.

choices.text: That 256 divides 768 exactly
choices.why: Any prefix length can be kept. Divisibility has nothing to do with what the coordinates carry.

choices.text: Whether their database has a column type for 256 numbers
choices.why: Storage can hold any length. The question is whether the shorter vector still finds the right documents.

prompt: How many bytes does one vector take with `dimensions=128`, stored as float32?
hint: dims.py printed the bytes for each size.

prompt: Match each way of getting a WordLlama vector to its recall@3 on the 24 questions, as dims.py measured.
hint: Cutting by hand without renormalising did worst.

pairs.left: cut to 64 by hand, not renormalised

prompt: At LiteLLM's sheet price of $0.020 per million tokens for text-embedding-3-small, what does it cost to embed 2 million chunks of 300 tokens each, in US dollars?
hint: First the total tokens, then divide by a million.

prompt: The sheet lists text-embedding-3-small at 0.020 and its batch price at 0.010 per million tokens. What does the lower price buy less of?
hint: How does the Batch API return results?

choices.text: Fewer dimensions in each vector
choices.why: The model and its vectors are the same; only how and when they are delivered changes.

choices.text: Speed: results come back later, within a day, instead of in the response
choices.why: Right. You upload a file of requests and collect the results afterwards.

choices.text: Accuracy, because batch requests use an older model
choices.why: The batch price is listed for the same model name. Nothing says a different model answers.

choices.text: Retries: failed batch requests are not retried
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about that, and it is not what the price difference is for.

prompt: Ana budgets $10.00 to embed a million 500-token documents with text-embedding-3-small. Six months later the bill is higher. Which explanation fits the lesson?
hint: What else gets embedded besides the documents, once?

choices.text: Overlapping chunks re-embedded text, and every user query was embedded too
choices.why: Right. Both add tokens the one-off calculation never counted.

choices.text: The SDK sends each vector twice, once as base64 and once as floats
choices.why: It asks for base64 only and decodes it locally. Only tokens are billed, not bytes.

choices.text: Vectors are billed per dimension, and 1,536 is more than expected
choices.why: An embedding API bills input tokens. The number of dimensions does not appear on the sheet's price.

choices.text: Retries of rate-limited requests were billed as successful ones
choices.why: A refused request returns no vector. The lesson's extra costs come from more text, not from refusals.

prompt: labembed was set to refuse the next two requests with 429. What did Ana's program see when it called `embeddings.create` once?
hint: Compare the program's output with the log.

choices.text: A RateLimitError on the first refusal
choices.why: The SDK retries 429 by itself, up to max_retries, before raising anything.

choices.text: Two warnings, then the vector
choices.why: Nothing was printed or raised about the refusals; they appear only in the server's log.

choices.text: A normal answer, a little late
choices.why: Right. Three requests reached the server; the program saw one successful call that took longer.

choices.text: An empty vector, because the request was refused
choices.why: The answer had all 384 numbers. The third attempt succeeded.

prompt: Which of these failures does the openai SDK retry by itself?
hint: Would sending the same request again change the answer?

choices.text: 400, because the input contained an empty string
choices.why: The request itself is wrong, so it would fail again. The log showed a single request for it.

choices.text: 401, because the key is wrong
choices.why: A wrong key stays wrong. The SDK raises AuthenticationError at once.

choices.text: 404, because the model name is unknown
choices.why: An unknown model stays unknown. The SDK raises NotFoundError at once.

choices.text: 429, because the account is over its rate limit
choices.why: Right. The request is fine and the moment is wrong, so waiting and retrying can succeed.

prompt: With three failures queued in labembed, put what happened during one call in order.
hint: max_retries is 2.
items: The first attempt is refused with 429
The SDK waits about a second
The first retry is refused with 429
The second retry is refused with 429
trap: There is no third retry: max_retries 2 means two retries after the first attempt, three requests in all.

prompt: Ana writes a nightly job that embeds every help article through the SDK. Which of these belong in it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about which failures each one prevents, and which it causes.

choices.text: Drop empty texts before building each batch
choices.why: Yes. One empty string makes the server refuse the whole request.

choices.text: Put each slice's vectors in the order of their index
choices.why: Yes. The index is what ties a vector to its text.

choices.text: Wrap each call in her own loop of three attempts
choices.why: No. The SDK already retries 429s; her loop would multiply the attempts on a provider that is already refusing.

choices.text: Ask lab-minilm for dimensions=128 to save space
choices.why: No. lab-minilm has one fixed size and refuses the parameter with a 400.

prompt: Match each exception the SDK raised in this lesson to the HTTP status behind it.
hint: One status never came up.

prompt: With the client's default settings, one call reaches the server at most ___ times before the SDK gives up on a 429.
hint: The first attempt, plus max_retries.
